title: Group Counseling for Children and Adolescents
welcome: A well-led group gives a young person something no individual session can: the discovery that they are not alone.
vignette: In a fourth-grade social-skills group, a quiet girl laughs at another child's joke, then freezes, unsure if she is allowed to belong. The group leader holds the moment. In circles, small moments teach the biggest lessons.
vignette_attr: A school group session, drawn from practice
description: The theory and practice of therapeutic groups with young people: group stages and dynamics, screening and composition, play-based and expressive formats, school-based group programs, and leading groups for grief, social skills, anger, and anxiety.
questions: What does the group provide that the individual cannot?
How do I lead a circle of children and hold each one?
When is a group harmful, and how do I prevent it?
importance: Peers are the natural change agents of childhood and adolescence
Groups deliver scarce counseling resources to more young people
Group experience rehearses the social world in miniature
misconceptions: that a group is just several individual sessions at once, when group dynamics are their own force
that any willing child belongs in any group, when screening and composition decide outcomes
figures: whose therapeutic factors explain why groups heal
who revealed the hidden dynamics beneath group life
who brought expressive, play-based depth to groups with children
outcomes: You will plan groups matched to age, purpose, and culture.
You will lead forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning.
You will select members who help rather than harm one another.
Manage group dynamics and difficult moments
You will handle scapegoating, dominance, and silence with skill.
You will use play and art as the group's language.
You will measure change and report it clearly.
modules: The factors name what we must deliberately create.
Dynamics are the weather the leader must read.
Who belongs and who does not
Composition is the first and most powerful intervention.
Art, stories, and ritual in the circle
Expression lets children say what words cannot.
Schools are where most young people can be reached.
Grief, anger, anxiety, and social-skills groups
Endings consolidate what the circle has built.
practicum: Participation in a live experiential group
Co-leading a short group with feedback
assessment: A full group proposal with screening plan
A recorded facilitation segment with critique
tips: Learn the stages so you never mistake storming for failure
Protect every member's dignity in the circle
Co-lead when you can; two eyes see more
integration: Group work multiplies every individual skill you learn in this programme.
faith: The circle echoes the community of faith; we lead it with the same hospitality.
closing: May the circles you lead become places where no young person feels alone again.
